For instance, if α is a real root of the integer polynomial A(x), we can represent α by the pair (A(x), I) where I is a interval with rational endpoints containing α but no other real roots of A(x). This is called the isolating interval representation of algebraic numbers. For instance, √2 can be represented as the pair (x² − 2, [1, 2]). Note that A(x) and I are both non-unique. We can make A(x) unique by insisting it to be the minimal polynomial of α (i.e., smallest degree primitive polynomial with positive leading coefficient), but that is too expensive to enforce. We can effective perform the 4 arithmetic operations on such representations, compare two such numbers, and so on. See [17, 86].
